approachQuestion.prompt:
One Processor
Simulate this rule for n jobs: when idle, choose the available unfinished job with shortest duration, ties by smaller ID; run it to completion without interruption. If none is available, jump to the next release time. Return execution IDs. Example: jobs [(0,5,0),(1,1,1),(1,2,2)] as (release,duration,ID) → [0,1,2].

1 ≤ n ≤ 200000. IDs are 0 through n−1, unique. Releases are integers from 0 to 1000000000; durations from 1 to 1000000000. Time fits 64 bits. Input is read-only and unsorted. The requested rule is fixed; do not optimize total completion time. Which approach best meets this contract?
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000. IDs are 0 through n−1, unique. Releases are integers from 0 to 1000000000; durations from 1 to 1000000000. Time fits 64 bits. Input is read-only and unsorted. The requested rule is fixed; do not optimize total completion time.

options.text: Sort a copy by release. At each idle decision, enqueue every released job in a min-heap keyed by (duration,ID). If it is empty, advance time to the next release and enqueue jobs there. Otherwise remove its minimum, append its ID, and advance time by its duration.
options.feedback: The heap contains exactly eligible unfinished jobs. Time advances only at completion or to the next release, so the rule is simulated without inspecting each time unit.

options.text: At every decision, scan all unfinished jobs for the best eligible one, or the next release if none is eligible.
options.feedback: This respects the rule but repeatedly scans jobs instead of preserving the eligible candidates.

options.text: Globally sort jobs by duration and execute in that order, waiting for each release.
options.feedback: In the example, job 0 is the only available job at time 0 and must start first.

options.text: Interrupt the running job whenever a shorter job arrives.
options.feedback: In the example, job 0 cannot be interrupted at time 1; the required scheduler is nonpreemptive.

Choose only among released jobs using duration then ID. If none is eligible, jump to the next release instead of iterating idle clock ticks. New arrivals during a running job wait until its nonpreemptive completion.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze A using iterative heapsort of a copied n-record array, a binary heap, and a forward release pointer. Let n be jobs. Time jumps are arithmetic operations, not loops through clock ticks. Output IDs are copied to a separate list. Choose the tightest time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Use the tightest worst-case bound for the whole input unless amortized or expected accounting is explicitly specified. Comparing or moving a record and arithmetic on machine words take constant time.

Exclude supplied input and returned output from auxiliary space. Count working arrays, queues, tables and call stacks. Output storage is separate and is not used as workspace. Heap repairs and traversals are iterative. No hashing is used unless explicitly stated.

options.text: O(n log(n+1)) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(n+T) time, O(n) auxiliary space, where T is final clock time
O(n log(n+1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Sort releases and insert/remove each job once, independent of clock magnitude.
details: The initial sort dominates O(n log(n+1)). Each job enters and leaves the eligible heap once. Clock magnitude affects arithmetic values but not iteration counts, and the copied jobs plus heap require O(n) working space. The n output writes are counted in time, excluded from space.
“O(n+T) time, O(n) auxiliary space, where T is final clock time”: The fixed method jumps across idle time and never iterates T ticks.
“O(n²) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: Each release is consumed once; heap choice avoids full scans.
“O(n log(n+1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The sorted copy and eligible queue are working storage.
